data.title: Footer
data.tagline: End the page with useful links, identity, and required information
data.description: A footer gives visitors another route to important pages and carries company details, legal links, contact information, or a final action. Organize links into clear groups and keep it useful rather than turning it into a second copy of the entire site.

use: A restrained final call to action
avoid: Repeat every navigation item without grouping
Use a huge footer to compensate for unclear navigation
Add a newsletter form with no explanation of what will be sent

lessonPractice.title: A site footer needs privacy, terms, help, and contact details, while a seven-day refund window directly affects purchase. How should it be organized?

options.label: Group supplementary links and contact paths, while keeping the refund window visible near purchase
options.feedback: The footer consolidates supplementary information, while decision-critical terms remain visible before action.

options.label: Copy every header navigation item and button into the footer and then add legal links
options.feedback: Mechanical repetition creates an unscannable link pile instead of serving needs at the end of the page.

options.label: Mention the refund window only inside a footer terms link to keep pricing cards clean
options.feedback: A refund limit changes the purchase decision, so hiding it at the bottom withholds key information before action.

data.agentPrompt: Group footer links into Product, Resources, Company, and Legal and provide a working contact path without copying the whole header. Keep purchase terms near pricing and CTAs, then check mobile grouping, external-link names, and dead links.

references.title: Web Page Footers 101: Design Patterns and When to Use Each
